title: Knowledge isn’t enough: chemophobia, chemical avoidance, and implications for chemistry education and outreach in China
content: Chemophobia can undermine informed engagement and discourage the pursuit of chemistry-related careers. This article reports on two linked survey studies in China, an underexamined context for chemophobia research. Study 1 (N = 787) examined the knowledge-based and evaluative factors associated with chemophobia, whereas Study 2 (N = 355) examined its association with chemical avoidance using an EPPM-informed model. In Study 1, higher toxicology knowledge but not general scientific literacy was associated with lower chemophobia, while risk–benefit evaluation and natural preference were associated with higher chemophobia. In Study 2, chemophobia was directly associated with chemical avoidance and showed significant indirect associations via higher perceived threat and lower perceived efficacy. The efficacy-related indirect association was smaller at higher toxicology knowledge levels, whereas the threat-related indirect association was larger at higher fear levels. Taken together, these findings indicate that knowledge-related variables alone provide an incomplete account of chemophobia and its association with chemical avoidance. Chemistry outreach and education may benefit from connecting chemical knowledge with risk–benefit evaluation, reflection on naturalness-based assumptions, and efficacy-building while exploring ways for the public to foster a more positive emotional connection with chemistry.
